title: The Room of the Undercroft
premise: Freya Crane, a folklorist cataloguing songs in the remote village of Hollowmere, records a lullaby the villagers refuse to sing twice—and that night the melted-down church bell rings across the valley. The bell's tolling marks an old covenant: every generation must return what it took, and in 1974 the village stole a child, Ivo Marsh, passing him off as a stillbirth to spare the church's reputation. Freya, it turns out, was that child, renamed and carried away by the folklorist who raised him; the bell has been ringing for him. To silence it, Freya must uncover the truth of his own theft, confront the dying woman who took him, and offer the village a justice it never gave Ivo's mother—returning himself, or something in his place, before the bell's final toll. He chooses to stay, taking Ivo's name and place among the dead and the living, and the bell falls silent only when the village, for the first time, sings the lullaby twice.
about_author: Paloma Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish records in the English countryside before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in bureaucratic evil—the sins small communities file away and forget.

chapters.title: Songs Not Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Freya Crane arrives in Hollowmere to record folk songs for an archive, charmed by the village until old Marta Tull begins a lullaby and is silenced mid-verse by her neighbors. Freya, whose POV opens the book, notes the fear beneath the courtesy. The emotional beat is unease disguised as hospitality.

chapters.title: The Bell That Was Not
chapters.summary: At midnight, a bell tolls from the roofless church tower, though parish records confirm the bell was melted down in 1911. Freya, sleepless and rational, walks to the church and finds fresh rope, worn stone, and a cold that moves against the wind. His certainty begins to crack; the beat is denial sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: What the Vestry Kept
chapters.summary: Freya searches the church vestry and finds a 1974 register with a page razored out, and a photograph of a young woman holding a swaddled bundle. The vicar's widow, Edith Parr, catches him and warns him to leave Hollowmere before the bell counts to twelve. The beat is the first glimpse of a buried crime.

chapters.title: Twelve Counts
chapters.summary: The bell rings eleven times that night and stops, and the village wakes changed—livestock still, wells tasting of iron. Edith tells Freya the bell tolls once a year for what was taken, but this year it is counting. Freya's POV carries mounting panic beneath his insistence on evidence.

chapters.title: Marta's Half-Song
chapters.summary: Freya coaxes Marta Tull into singing the lullaby's first verse alone in her kitchen; she weeps and calls him 'Ivo' before her daughter hustles her out of the room. Freya dismisses it as dementia but cannot shake the name, which he finds scratched inside the church tower. The beat is uncanny recognition.

chapters.title: The Mother in the Photograph
chapters.summary: In the county archive Freya traces the photograph to Nell Marsh, a servant girl who died in 1975, and a birth record for Ivo Marsh marked 'stillborn' in a hand that differs from the rest of the page. The falsification is obvious to his trained eye. The beat is the scholar's thrill curdling into horror.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Raised Him
chapters.summary: Freya calls his adoptive mother, folklorist Ruth Crane, who goes silent on the phone and then says only: 'Don't go back to Hollowmere, Freya.' He realizes she visited the village in 1974, the year he was born. The beat is betrayal dawning—the person he loved most is inside the crime.

chapters.title: The Village Closes
chapters.summary: Freya tries to leave and finds the road out blocked by a fallen oak no storm felled, phones dead, the bus route suspended 'for repairs.' The villagers are polite, watchful, and will not meet his eyes. The beat is claustrophobia—the archive becomes a trap.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Edith Parr, dying and past fear, tells Freya that in 1974 the vicar declared Nell Marsh's living baby dead to protect the church from scandal, and that a visiting folklorist carried the child away. Freya does not yet let himself understand. The beat is the horror of a crime committed for respectability.

chapters.title: The Name on the Tape
chapters.summary: Freya plays Ruth's old field recordings from 1974 and hears her voice interviewing Nell Marsh—and beneath it, a newborn crying. Ruth's label reads 'Ivo M. — placed, with the village's consent.' Freya's POV fractures; he speaks the truth aloud for the first time. The beat is identity collapse.

chapters.title: What the Bell Wants
chapters.summary: The bell tolls a ninth time, and that night Freya dreams in Nell Marsh's voice, walking the churchyard, looking for a child who was never buried. He wakes with churchyard clay under his fingernails. The beat is the supernatural becoming intimate and bodily.

chapters.title: The Grave That Is Empty
chapters.summary: Freya and Marta's daughter, the reluctant ally Sian Tull, open the Marsh infant plot and find it empty—no coffin, ever. Sian confesses her family has kept the village's silence for fifty years out of fear. The beat is complicity exposed; the village's guilt becomes the story's true monster.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Freya wants police, lawyers, records; Sian explains the crime is beyond any court now—everyone culpable is dead or dying, and the statute of conscience runs longer than any statute of law. The bell demands a different accounting. The beat is the theme crystallized: the law cannot reach this, something else must.

chapters.title: Ruth Comes Home
chapters.summary: Ruth Crane arrives unannounced, old and ill, having known the bell would call her back. She admits she took the baby believing she was saving him, and that she has dreaded this return for fifty years. The beat is love against duty—her love for Freya set against what she owes the village and the dead.

chapters.title: The Tenth Toll
chapters.summary: The bell tolls ten times and the village begins to fail: frost in June, the churchyard yew bleeding sap, villagers sleepwalking toward the tower each night. Freya realizes the counting will finish whether he is ready or not. The beat is the clock becoming audible.

chapters.title: Nell's Verse
chapters.summary: Marta Tull, in a lucid hour, teaches Freya the lullaby's full words—Nell Marsh's own song, a promise to return to her child. Freya sings it back to her and the room goes still; the dead, it seems, are listening. The beat is grief transfigured into ritual, the folklorist finally believing.

chapters.title: The Offering Refused
chapters.summary: The village elders propose the old solution: bury something of Ivo's—a lock of hair, Ruth's recordings—in the empty grave and let the matter rest as they rested everything. Freya refuses; a token is another theft, a lie sung twice. The beat is the moral climax of the theme: half-justice is no justice.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Toll
chapters.summary: The bell tolls eleven times and does not stop ringing between counts; the tower doors stand open onto darkness. Ruth, failing fast, begs Freya to run and never look back, and he holds her and tells her he is not running from his own name. The beat is love and duty finally aligned.

chapters.title: The Room of the Undercroft
chapters.summary: Beneath the tower, Freya finds the undercroft room where Nell's belongings were locked away in 1974—her letters, her unlived life, filed like his own archive. He understands the bell was never vengeful; it is a mother's song, still counting the steps home. The beat is terror resolving into terrible tenderness.

chapters.title: What Freya Returns
chapters.summary: At the twelfth toll, Freya lays himself in the empty grave's open mouth—his name, his history, the self called Freya Crane—surrendering it to Nell Marsh and taking up Ivo's. Ruth, Sian, and the village witness; the darkness in the tower receives him without cruelty. The beat is sacrifice as restitution, not punishment.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Dawn finds Ivo Marsh alive in the churchyard, changed but whole, and the bell silent at last. He leads the village in singing Nell's lullaby once, then, breaking fifty years of fear, twice. Ruth dies peacefully that autumn, forgiven; Sian burns the old silences in the vestry stove. The beat is release.

chapters.title: The Archive of the Living
chapters.summary: Ivo stays in Hollowmere as its record-keeper, restoring the razored page with the truth in his own hand and recording every villager's account, however shameful, for whoever comes after. On quiet nights he sings the lullaby twice, and the valley keeps its silence—not the silence of fear, but of a debt paid. The beat is justice outside the law, completed.
